True Crime. The literary genre that recounts actual criminal events with the narrative technique of novels, raising questions about representation, responsibility, and whether real suffering can be art.

It's distinct from detective fiction, which invents its mysteries, and from crime journalism, which reports daily in newspapers. True crime has narrative depth. It develops characters. It has literary ambition. As a recognizable genre, true crime was crystallized by Truman Capote's In Cold Blood in 1966. Capote interviewed perpetrators, victims' families, investigators, and then reconstructed real events using fictional techniques. The book sold millions of copies. It was adapted into a landmark film. It legitimized the form. Before In Cold Blood, this kind of ambitious reporting about real crimes didn't have a name or a tradition. Afterward it did.

The genre exploded in popularity in the late twentieth century and into the twenty-first. Podcasts, streaming documentaries, television series—true crime became a dominant popular genre. Audiences are drawn to morbid curiosity, to fascination with criminal psychology, to interest in where the justice system fails and why. Contemporary works include Michelle McNamara's I'll Be Gone in the Dark, John Douglas's The Killer Across the Table, and the series Serial and Making a Murderer.

But true crime raises persistent ethical questions. Is it voyeuristic? Does it exploit real trauma? Do literary techniques distort or illuminate truth? The genre also raises questions about representation and power. Whose crimes receive literary treatment? True crime often amplifies cases involving white perpetrators or privileged victims. The visibility the genre grants is not distributed evenly.

Yet true crime can serve investigative functions. Michelle McNamara's I'll Be Gone in the Dark led to an arrest and conviction. The line between literature and activism becomes ambiguous. The work of retelling becomes the work of justice. True crime asks readers to think about murder, investigation, criminal psychology, the machinery of law—and to do it through compelling narrative. That power to compel, to make real crime into something you cannot look away from, is what makes the ethical questions matter so much.
